title: Unraveling the Catalytic Mechanism and Substrate Selectivity of HDAC10: A Dual-Filter Approach for Polyamine Deacetylation

sections.abstract: The histone deacetylase (HDAC) family plays a crucial role in regulating acetylation-dependent cellular processes, with dysregulation linked to diseases ranging from cancer to neurodegeneration. HDAC10, the sole polyamine deacetylase in the HDAC family, uniquely influences pathologies such as tumor immunity, autophagy, inflammation, virus infection, silicosis, etc . Despite its therapeutic potential, the molecular basis of HDAC10’s catalytic activity and substrate selectivity remains poorly understood, hindering rational drug design. Here, we address this gap by integrating density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics simulation to systematically investigate HDAC10’s catalytic activity and substrate selectivity. Utilizing a 330-atom quantum cluster model, we evaluated five distinct reaction pathways. The double-proton transfer mechanism (D’D) is dominant, featuring a concerted double-proton transfer step and a rate-limiting protonation of the substrate’s amide nitrogen (20.4 kcal/mol barrier). Substrate selectivity arises from synergistic effects: N 8 -acetylspermidine benefits from enhanced binding via active-site hydrogen-bond networks and reduced catalytic barriers compared to N 1 -acetylspermidine, which suffers from electrostatic repulsion and dynamic instability. This study provides the first atomic-resolution framework for HDAC10’s catalysis and selectivity, resolving long-standing mechanistic ambiguities. By identifying critical interactions governing substrate recognition and turnover, our work establishes a foundation for designing isoform-specific HDAC10 inhibitors, offering strategic avenues to target its roles in disease.
sections.introduction:
Acetylation modifications play a critical role in regulating protein function and polyamine metabolism, impacting both fundamental biological processes and the development of various diseases. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) are key enzymes that modulate these acetylation states. They comprise a family of 18 isoforms categorized into four classes: Class I (HDAC1, 2, 3, and 8), Class IIa (HDAC4, 5, 7, and 9), Class IIb (HDAC6 , and 10 − ), Class III (SIRT1–7), − and Class IV (HDAC11). As has been discovered recently, HDAC10 is unique in functioning as the sole polyamine deacetylase in the family with remarkable substrate specificity, and the resolution of its crystal structure provides valuable structural insights. It specifically hydrolyzes N 8 -acetylspermidine and cleaves the amide bond with k cat / K M of more than 2 orders of magnitude over that of N 1 -acetylspermidine ( Figure A). − This exceptional selectivity underscores HDAC10’s specialized role in polyamine metabolism and its potential role as a target in anticancer therapies. − HDAC10 is also of crucial physiological and pathological importance by associating with diseases, such as antitumor immunity, autophagy, , inflammation, , virus infection, and silicosis, which further underscores its therapeutic potential.

(A) Deacetylation reactions of substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine and N 1 -acetylspermidine catalyzed by HDAC10, respectively. (B) Crystal structure of ‘humanized’ (A24E, D94A) zebrafish HDAC10 (Y307F) with the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine (PDB ID: 7KUQ ). (C) Schematic illustration of the active site of HDAC10. Thick red dashed lines represent the coordination bonds with ions and thin blue dashed lines represent hydrogen bonds.

The catalytic activity of HDAC10 is governed by its polyamine deacetylase (PDAC) domain, which contains several key catalytic elements ( Figure B). The sequentially conserved dyads His136/Asp172 and His137/Gln179 are of crucial importance within this domain ( Figure S1 ). The absence of either analogous histidine residue in HDAC8 significantly alters the reaction activity. Asp172 and Gln179 form hydrogen bond interactions with the δH atoms of the histidines, respectively ( Figure C and Figure S2A ). A Zn 2+ ion plays a pivotal role by polarizing the substrate carbonyl group and coordinating a water molecule, thereby promoting nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl group from the water molecule ( Figure C and Figure S2A ). Adjacent to the PDAC domain is the catalytically inactive domain ΨDAC ( Figure B), which is sequentially analogous to the PDAC domain ( Figure S1 ). However, the key residues responsible for zinc binding and deacetylation are not conserved in it ( Figure S1 ).

A deep understanding of the catalytic mechanisms of HDAC10 is crucial for the rational design of drugs and other therapeutic applications targeting it. The catalytic mechanisms of other zinc-dependent HDACs, such as HDAC1, , HDAC8, , and HDAC6 , have been extensively studied. The mechanisms typically begin with one of the two histidines acting as a general base to deprotonate the Zn 2+ -coordinated water molecule. This is either followed or accompanied by the nucleophilic attack of the resulting hydroxide ion (OH – ) on the carbonyl carbon of the substrate, forming an intermediate tetrahedral complex. Subsequently, proton transfer occurs, culminating in the cleavage of the amide bond to complete the reaction. The mechanisms followed by different HDACs differ in several aspects. Key differences include whether the histidines are initially protonated only at the δN position of histidine (HID) or at both δN and εN positions (HIP), respectively ( Figure S2B ), which histidine acts as the general base to deprotonate the water molecule, whether the intermediate deprotonated water is metastable or not, whether and how the hydroxyl group in the intermediate tetrahedron is deprotonated, and what are the pathways that the intermediate protons adopt during the process, etc . These differences have led to several different mechanisms for the members of the HDAC family. , −

Being one of the most recently discovered HDACs, HDAC10 is among the least studied and understood members within the HDAC family. How does it lower the high free energy barrier of the deacetylation reaction (estimated to be 43.1 ∼ 47.1 kcal/mol, Figure S2C,D )? Whether it employs a similar catalytic mechanism to its family members? , What is the molecular mechanism of its substrate selectivity? These questions remain to be answered. The lack of detailed mechanistic insights significantly hinders further investigation into HDAC10’s physiological roles and its potential as a therapeutic target.

Quantum mechanical (QM) calculations have proven to be a powerful tool, offering unparalleled insights into the electronic structure, reactivity, and dynamical behavior of chemical and biological systems. , − In this work, we conducted a systematic investigation into the molecular mechanisms governing the catalytic activity and substrate selectivity of HDAC10. Five potential catalytic mechanisms have been investigated. Each mechanism is characterized by distinct protonation states of the catalytic dyads and proton transfer pathways, representing the most comprehensive microscopic mechanistic study to date on the deacetylation reaction catalyzed by HDAC10. It has been shown that the size of model used for QM calculations significantly impacts the predicted mechanism, known as the “truncation effect”. To minimize the effect, we employed a large cluster model containing 330 atoms (Model-330) for the investigation ( Figure A). An even larger model with 559 atoms (Model-559), whose QM calculation is enabled by the eXtended ONIOM (XO) methodology, , shows a similar configuration ( Figure B), indicating that Model-330 is large enough to include all relevant participants. Among the mechanisms investigated, the double-proton mechanism is identified as the predominant pathway due to its lowest free energy barrier. This mechanism features a concerted double-proton transfer process, where the rate-limiting step is the protonation of the amide nitrogen in the substrate, which is evidently different from the case in HDAC8. Regarding substrate selectivity, our analysis reveals that the enzyme selectively catalyzes substrates based not only on their affinity but also on the energetic landscape they present during the catalytic cycle. Further analysis on the electronic nature and dynamic properties of protein–substrate interactions provides a deeper understanding on how HDAC10 achieves its catalytic efficiency and selectivity.

Optimized structures of the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex of Model-330 (A), Model-559 (B) and Model-230 (C). His136 and His137 are kept in the HID state. The calculations are conducted by using B3LYP-D3­(BJ)/(6-31G­(d,p), SDD) for the two smaller models and by using the XO methodology XO2­[H = B3LYP-D3­(BJ)/(6-31G­(d,p), 6-311+G­(d,p), SDD):L = PM6-D3)] for Model-559. Carbon atoms are pink for the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine, green for the three residues coordinated to Zn 2+ , blue for the His136, His137, and Tyr307, orange for other common residues in both Model-330 and Model-559, and purple for residues only in Model-559. Six distances are measured to describe the active site geometry ( d 1 : distance between Zn 2+ and Asp174; d 2 : distance between Zn 2+ and His176; d 3 : distance between Zn 2+ and Asp267; d 4 : distance between Zn 2+ and the oxygen atom of the coordinated water molecule; d 5 : distance between Zn 2+ and the acetyl oxygen of the substrate; d 6 : the length of amide bond of the substrate). Distances are given in Å.
sections.methods:
Three cluster models of the active site of HDAC10 were established out of the crystallographic structure of ‘humanized’ (A24E, D94A) zebrafish HDAC10 (Y307F) in complex with the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine (PDB ID: 7KUQ ). The residue Phe307 was manually mutated back to the wild type Tyr307. Hydrogens were added using the H++ program. The protonation states of His136 and His137 in the initial enzyme–substrate (ES) complex including HID136/HID137 (DD), HIP136/HID137 (PD), and HID136/HIP137 (DP) were used to investigate different mechanisms.

Model-230 was built in reference to the analogical systems, and was further expanded to Model-330 and Model-559 to include more distant residues and ions, , respectively. Atoms in some residues connected to C α atom were deleted and the dangling bonds were capped with hydrogen atoms (see the Supporting Information ). Besides the amino acid residues, N 8 -acetylspermidine or N 1 -acetylspermidine, three key water molecules, and the catalytic Zn 2+ ion were included in the three models. Both Model-330 and Model-559 contain a K + ion near the active site, which was reported to be important for determining energy barrier of the deacetylation reaction in HDAC8. ,

In the HID136/HID137 (DD) protonation state with N 8 -acetylspermidine, Model-330 has a zero net charge, and 21 atoms at the boundary of the model (C α atoms of the truncated residues and the K + ion) were frozen during optimization to stabilize the active site structure ( Figure S3A ). Model-559 has a net charge of −1 and 26 atoms were frozen during optimization ( Figure S3B ). Model-230 has a net charge of −1 and 13 atoms were frozen during optimization ( Figure S3C ).

Quantum mechanical (QM) calculations were performed using Gaussian 16 B.01 software package with the keyword ‘G09Defaults’. Structure optimization, frequency calculations, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) path analysis, and potential energy surface scan were performed using B3LYP-D3­(BJ) , hybrid functional along with basis set 6-31G­(d,p) for C, H, O, N atoms, 6-311+G­(d,p) , for S atoms if exists, and the Stuttgart ECP (or SDD) for the Zn 2+ and K + ions. The polarizable continuum model (PCM) was employed to consider the environment with a dielectric constant ε = 4 for optimization, frequency calculation, IRC path analysis, and single point energy calculations, which is appropriate for the enzyme active site. All transition states have only one imaginary frequency and the vibration motion of the imaginary frequency corresponds to the reaction pathway. All minima have no imaginary frequency.

For single point energy calculations, the MN15, M06-2X, PBE0-D3­(BJ), and ωB97X-D functionals were used with a larger basis set def2-TZVP. Different functionals brought quantitative differences in the free energy values, but no qualitative difference was found ( Figure S14A–C and Table S1 ). The selection of dielectric constant ε (either 4 or 1) also brings no qualitative difference ( Figure S14A–C ). The thermal correction for Gibbs free energy was calculated at 310 K using Grimme’s quasi rigid-rotor-harmonic-oscillator (quasi-RRHO) method with the Shermo software, which was appropriate for flexible systems ( Table S3 ). The loose convergence criterion was utilized in the potential energy surface scan and structure optimization of INT-DDY.

The high-level method of the XO methodology was the same as that used for full-system QM calculation. Semiempirical PM6 including Grimme’s dispersion correction (zero-damping) was used as the low-level method, which is of satisfactory accuracy without using PCM.

The independent gradient model based on Hirshfeld partition (IGMH) method was chosen for weak interaction analysis between the substrate and the enzyme. The weak interactions within 5 Å of the substrate and three water molecules were analyzed using Multiwfn , software with a precise grid spacing of 0.15 Bohr. Graph generation was performed using VMD and UCSF ChimeraX. The following formula calculated the binding energy between the enzyme and the substrate: Δ E bind = E complex − E enzyme − E substrate + E BSSE where basis set superposition error (BSSE) was considered in the binding energy calculations by counterpoise correction. The binding energy was calculated at the B3LYP-D3­(BJ)/6-311+G­(2d,p) level and decomposed by the sobEDAw method to the four parts, including electrostatic, exchange-repulsion, orbital, and dispersion energy: Δ E bind = Δ E els + Δ E xrep + Δ E orb + E disp which is analogous to the symmetric-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT). The following formula was used to calculate residue contribution to the binding energy: Δ Δ E = Δ E bind ( whole cluster ) − Δ E bind ( without residues )

A negative ΔΔ E indicated a favorable contribution from the excluded residues. The catalytic water molecule coordinated with the Zn 2+ ion was considered a part of the substrate, and the two bridging water molecules were treated as a part of Glu274.

The Eyring equation is used to derive free energy barrier (Δ G ‡ ) from the rate constant ( k TST ): k TST = σ k B T h e − Δ G ‡ / ( R T ) Where σ = 1, k B = 1.3806503 × 10 –23 J/K, T = 310.15 K, h = 6.6260696 × 10 –34 J·s, and R = 8.3144719 J/mol/K.

To calculate the deuterium kinetic isotope effect (KIE), a frequency analysis for ES-DD and TS3-DD were conducted with iso = 2 for the transferred hydrogen atom, respectively. The rate constant with deuterium ( k D ) was derived from the free energy barrier by using the Eyring equation and the ratio k H / k D is the KIE value, where k H is the rate constant with for the protium (H) isotopologue.

We tested our eXtended ONIOM (XO) , methodology for the large cluster models with more than 300 atoms, which divides a system into overlapping fragments to enable QM calculation of large structures with little loss in accuracy. − Model-330 and Model-559 were calculated, respectively. XO fragmentation scheme was derived for each structure as follows. A model structure was first divided into several minimal units (see Figure S4A,B for definition). Every unit expands itself to include all units within a distance of 2.5 Å to form a primitive “egg”. All primitive eggs were compared and an egg was removed if it was a subset of the other egg in the egg collection. Combination of all existing primitive eggs results in an XO fragmentation scheme for an estimation of the energy and the atomic force of the full system according to the inclusion-exclusion principle (IEP): | A 1 ∪ A 2 ∪ ··· ∪ A n | = ∑ i = 1 n | A i | − ∑ i < j | A i ∩ A j | + ∑ i < j < k | A i ∩ A j ∩ A k | + ··· + ( − 1 ) n − 1 | A 1 ∩ A 2 ∩ ··· ∩ A n | = ∑ i = 1 n | A i | − ∑ m = 2 n ( − 1 ) m | A m D |

The A m D represented all derived terms for a given m , which contains n ! ( n − m ) ! possible intersections of m primitive terms out of the total of n primitive terms. Full-system energy E full was approximated by XO energy E XO which is linear combination of energy of the fragments: E full ≈ E XO = ∑ i = 1 n E A i − ∑ m = 2 n ( − 1 ) m E A m D

XO n is a straightforward generalization of ONIOM n by IEP to allow for a combination of n levels of methods. Two levels of methods were used in the XO calculation (XO2). The XO2 energy of the system is used to approximate the full-system energy at the high level of method calculated as the following formula: E full ( high ) ≈ E XO 2 ( high ) = E XO ( high ) − E XO ( low ) + E full ( low ) Where E full (high) is the full-system energy at the high level of method that is inaccessible due to the too large size of the system, E XO2 (high) is the XO2 energy derived from the high and low levels of methods, E XO (high) is the XO energy calculated with the high level of method, E XO (low) is the XO energy calculated with the low level of method, and E full (low) is the full-system energy calculated with the low level of method. A good selection of high and low levels of methods and a good XO fragmentation scheme could provide a good E XO2 (high) that is close to E full (high). Atomic forces were calculated accordingly that are the negative gradient of the XO2 energy with respect to atomic positions.

The initial ES complex structure was pretreated as described above to add hydrogen atoms, to mutate the residue back to the wild-type system, and to decide the protonation states for titratable residues. The missing residues including Gly435, Ala589, Ala590, Lys591, Thr592, and Arg593 were added through PDBFixer. His136 and His137 were single-protonated with a hydrogen bound to the delta nitrogen (HID136/HID137) according to our QM calculations results (Mechanisms D’D/DD’/DDY). MD simulations were performed using GROMACS package version 2019.3 with AMBER ff14SB force field for the protein HDAC10 and the generalized Amber force field (GAFF) for substrates N 8 -acetylspermidine and N 1 -acetylspermidine. The restrained electrostatic potential charges (RESP2(0.5)) of the substrate were calculated using Multiwfn , software at B3LYP-D3­(BJ) , /def2-TZVP level and the topology files were generated using Sobtop software. The LJ12-6 parameters proposed by Zhang and co-workers were used for the zinc and potassium ions. The complex was placed within a rectangular box and the distance between the complex surface and the wall of the box was greater than 15 Å. Periodic boundary condition was used in all three dimensions. The translation and rotation of the mass center of the complex were removed during simulation. Water molecules were filled into the simulation box with the TIP3P water model and NaCl counterions were added to neutralize the system and to achieve a concentration of 0.15 mol/L ( Figure S15A ). The system underwent energy minimization using the conjugate gradient (CG) method followed by 300 ps of position-restrained MD simulation, in which the atoms on the complex, and the Zn 2+ and K + ions were restrained. Finally, the whole system was simulated for 1000 ns at 310 K with the bonds connected to the hydrogen constrained using the LINCS algorithm. A time step of 2 fs was utilized. The V-rescale thermostat with a time constant of 0.2 ps was applied to maintain a constant temperature of 310 K in the system, while the solute and the solvent were coupled to different thermostats. The Parrinello-Rahman barostat was applied to maintain a constant pressure of 1 atm for the 1000 ns production MD simulations. The Berendsen barostat was used for the position-restrained MD simulations. Electrostatic and LJ interactions within 10 Å were calculated explicitly, while the long-range Coulomb interactions beyond 10 Å were treated with the particle mesh Ewald (PME) method. Each system has three production replicas for a better sampling.

The sequences of zebrafish HDAC10 (zHDAC10), human HDAC10 (hHDAC10), zebrafish HDAC6 (zHDAC6), and human HDAC6 (hHDAC6) were obtained from UniProt accession codes F1QCV2 , Q969S8 , F8W4B7, and Q9UBN7 , respectively. ClustalW algorithm was utilized and the figure of sequence alignment ( Figure S1 ) was generated at the ESPript Web site.
sections.results:
Cluster models offer an efficient means of accurately describing the complex environments of catalytic active sites and have been successfully applied in theoretical studies on enzyme catalytic mechanisms. , Crucially, the size of the cluster model plays a pivotal role in these studies, as it directly influences the reliability and precision of the mechanistic insights derived. The previous study on HDAC8 has demonstrated that varying the size of the QM regions can lead to different catalytic mechanisms, with larger QM regions generally yielding results more consistent with experimental data. In this work, we constructed three cluster models of different sizes −230, 330, and 559 atoms, designated as Model-230, Model-330, and Model-559 ( Figure ), respectivelybased on the crystal structure of ‘humanized’ zebrafish HDAC10 (PDB ID: 7KUQ ) bound to the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine, with the mutation of Y307F restored (see the Methods section for details).

Model-230 is the smallest among the three model structures ( Figure C), designed based on the framework used in a recent study on HDAC6. Although this model incorporates both catalytic dyads, His136/Asp172 and His137/Gln179, it does not include the K + ion. Model-330 was constructed by expanding Model-230 to incorporate additional surrounding amino acid residues and cofactors, specifically the K + ion and half of its coordinated residues, to better represent the environment of the catalytic active site ( Figure A). The third model, Model-559, encompasses all residues coordinating with the K + ion ( Figure B) and was employed to evaluate whether Model-330 provides a sufficiently accurate description of the active site.

Each model structure was optimized using the B3LYP-D3­(BJ) method with boundary atoms fixed ( Figure S3 ) to investigate how cluster size influences the local geometry of the active site in the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex. The standard Gaussian software was utilized for the geometric optimization of Model-230 and Model-330.

Because Model-559 exceeds the computational limit of conventional geometric optimization methods, we utilized the XO methodology that is implemented in a newly developed code ( https://github.com/wengjingwei35/g16XO ). , This methodology enables efficient parallel computation across 8 nodes, allowing us to complete the geometric optimization of Model-559 within a reasonable time frame. The XO calculation settings for Model-559 were validated via a force error test , ( Figure S4 , see more details in the Methods section). The settings were also validated by Model-330, as the XO-optimized structure exhibited high geometric consistency with the full-system optimization result ( Figure A and Figure S5A,B ). The geometric criterion used for comparison involves the key distances between the Zn 2+ ion and the five coordinated atoms on Asp174, His176, Asp267, the coordinated water molecule, and the acetyl oxygen of the substrate, respectively ( d 1 ∼ d 5 , Figure S5A ), as well as the length of the amide bond to be cleaved in the deacetylation reaction ( d 6 , Figure S5A ).

The optimized structures of Model-230, Model-330, and Model-559 exhibit strong geometric agreement in four of the coordination bonds and the amide bond ( d 1 ∼ d 4 , Figure and Figure S5 ), with a maximum deviation of 0.07 Å across three models. However, Model-230 ( Figure C and Figure S5C ) displays significant distortion in d 5 , the distance between the Zn 2+ ion and the acetyl oxygen of the substrate ( Figure A and Figure S5A ). In Model-230, d 5 increases sharply to 3.76 Å ( Figure C and Figure S5C ), indicating a weakened coordination bond. By contrast, d 5 measures 2.47 Å in Model-330 ( Figure A and Figure S5A ), 2.30 Å in Model-559 ( Figure B and Figure S5D ), 2.21Å in the Y307F mutant of the ES complex crystal structure ( Figure S6A ) and 2.26 Å in the wild-type enzyme–product (EP) complex crystal structure ( Figure S6B ). The distortion underscores that Model-230, while computationally efficient, fails to adequately represent the active site geometry required for mechanistic studies of HDAC10. Consequently, Model-330 was selected for subsequent QM calculation studies, as it achieves an optimal balance between computational efficiency and accuracy.

We next explored the catalytic mechanisms of the deacetylation reaction in HDAC10. Starting from the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex, where the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine is bound to the active site, the reaction begins with the deprotonation of a catalytic water molecule. This step is mediated by one of two histidine residues in the active site, with either His136 or His137 acting as a general base. The histidines feature the presence of protonated δ-nitrogen (δN) atoms to stabilize the catalytic dyads, while their ε-nitrogen (εN) positions can adopt either a deprotonated (to form HID) or protonated (to form HIP) state ( Figure S2B ). Crucially, only histidine residues with an unprotonated εN position can act as general bases to initiate the reaction. To systematically evaluate their roles, we considered five distinct protonation state combinations: HID136/HID137 (DD), HIP136/HID137 (PD), HID136/HIP137 (DP), HIE136/HID137 (ED) and HID136/HIE137 (DE). These configurations were systematically analyzed to assess their influence on the reaction mechanism.

QM calculations reveal that the ES complex with the DD protonation state (ES-DD) results in a stable penta-coordination around the Zn 2+ ion ( Figure A and Figure S5A ), consistent with the experimental observations in the crystal structure of the Y307F mutant ( Figure S6A ). However, further protonation of either histidine (PD or DP) leads to a quadra-coordinated Zn 2+ ion, where the substrate’s coordination bond with the Zn 2+ ion is weakened, increasing the bond length to 3.45 Å and 3.15 Å in the ES-PD ( Figure S7A ) and ES-DP ( Figure S7H ) complexes, respectively. A similar quadra-coordinated Zn 2+ ion has been observed in the ES complex of HDAC6.

In the ES-ED state, His136 is protonated at the εN position, which results in a quadra-coordinated Zn 2+ ion similar to that in the ES-PD state. The substrate’s coordination bond with Zn 2+ is significantly weakened ( d 5 = 3.50 Å, Figure S8A ). However, unlike the ES-PD state, the ES-ED state lacks a proton at the δN position of His136, which destabilizes the system by disrupting its hydrogen bond interaction with Asp172. Similarly, the ES-DE state features His137 protonated at the εN position, with a quadra-coordinated Zn 2+ ion and weakened substrate interaction ( d 5 = 3.15 Å, Figure S8B ) resembling those of the DP state. This state is also destabilized due to loss of hydrogen bonding with Gln179. Given the higher instability of both ES-ED (relative to ES-PD) and ES-DE (relative to ES-DP), we exclude these states from subsequent analyses.

Based on these findings, we identify four distinctive intermediate configurations for water deprotonation in HDAC10, corresponding to the deprotonated εN position of His136 in the D’D (i) and DP (ii) states and that of His137 in the DD’ (iii) and PD (iv) states. Here, the apostrophe notation (’) denotes the histidine residue actively engaged in water deprotonation (e.g., D’D signifies His136 as the catalytic base in the DD state). In consequence, we propose four distinct catalytic mechanisms for HDAC10-mediated deacetylation, categorized by the deprotonating histidine and labeled as D’D, DD’, PD, and DP. The corresponding reaction pathways, including all the relevant intermediates and transition states, are illustrated in Figure . Notably, the ES-DD state may bypass a unique intermediate state INT-DDY, leading to the fifth mechanism DDY, which is discussed in detail below.

Detailed deacetylation reaction mechanisms catalyzed by HDAC10 with the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine. (A) Mechanisms D’D, DD’, and DDY. (B) Mechanisms PD and DP.

Mechanism D’D begins with the water deprotonation facilitated by HID136, which proceeds concurrently with the nucleophilic attack of the generated OH – on the acetyl carbon. The corresponding transition state, TS1-D’D ( Figure A), exhibits an effective free reaction barrier of 15.0 kcal/mol ( Figure A). The resulting intermediate INT1-D’D ( Figure B) adopts a local tetrahedral structure centered at the acetyl carbon, marking a substantial transformation by converting from planar sp 2 hybridization to sp 3 hybridization. This geometric shift reflects the transformation of the CO double bond in the acetyl group to a C–O single bond ( Figures A and B). In this mechanism, HID136 acts as a general base, critically stabilizing the transition state and enhancing the nucleophilic attack to drive catalysis.

(A–I) Structures of the intermediate states (INT), the transition states (TS), and the enzyme–product (EP) complex for the catalysis of substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine in Mechanism D’D/DD’ are calculated with B3LYP-D3­(BJ)/(6-31G­(d,p), SDD). Distances are given in Å. The only imaginary frequency of every TS is denoted at the bottom left of the corresponding structure.

(A) Energy landscapes for Mechanisms D’D, DD’, and DDY are calculated with ωB97X-D/(def2-TZVP, SDD). (B) Energy landscapes for Mechanisms PD and DP are obtained by ωB97X-D/(def2-TZVP, SDD). The thermal correction for Gibbs free energy (Grimme’s quasi-RRHO method at 310 K) is given in parentheses.

Protonation of the amide nitrogen of the substrate is crucial for the cleavage of the amide bond in the following catalytic steps. Direct migration of the hydroxyl hydrogen of the tetrahedral intermediate complex to the amide nitrogen is unlikely to occur because the transition state has a very high free energy ( Figure S9 ). Among indirect pathways, the protonated side chain of His136 in the INT1-D’D state is positioned distally from the amide nitrogen (∼3.76 Å), precluding its role as a general acid for direct protonation of the amide nitrogen. For comparison, the εN position of His137 resides closer to the amide nitrogen ( Figure B). Computational analysis reveals that INT1-D’D rearranges to INT2-DD through a double-proton transfer process ( Figure A): the proton from His136 migrates to the hydroxyl group of the intermediate tetrahedron, concertedly with the transfer of the proton on the hydroxyl group to His137. This step surmounts the TS2-D’D transition state ( Figure C), yielding the INT2-DD intermediate ( Figure D). Here, His137’s εN position acquires a proton, which is ready to protonate the amide nitrogen as it is only 2.41 Å away ( Figure D).

Careful inspection of the geometries further demonstrates that the amine bond length progressively increases from 1.33 Å ( d 6 , Figure A) in the ES-DD state to 1.45 Å in INT1-D’D ( Figure B) and 1.46 Å in INT2-DD ( Figure D), reflecting bond destabilization. This elongation correlates with the HID136/HID137-assisted stepwise water deprotonation, which drives the progression of the overall deacetylation reaction.

In contrast, Mechanism DD’ initializes through HID137-mediated water deprotonation, where HID137 functions as a general base. The system passes through the TS1-DD’ transition state ( Figure I) and transforms directly to the INT2-DD intermediate ( Figure D). Notably, the free reaction barrier of TS1-DD’ rises to 19.7 kcal/mol (purple dashed line, Figure A). This suggests that the deprotonated histidine HID137, while functional, has a weaker proton-acquiring ability than HID136, and is less effective in stabilizing the transition state and promoting the nucleophilic attack.

After water deprotonation, Mechanisms D’D and DD’ converge and proceed through identical subsequent steps. The protonated His137 in the INT2-DD intermediate acts as a general acid to facilitate the protonation of the amide nitrogen in the substrate. By overcoming a free energy barrier of 20.4 kcal/mol (relative to the initial ES-DD complex, TS3-DD), the amine bond further elongates to 1.60 Å in the resulting INT3-DD state ( d 6 in Figure F), indicating further weakening. Finally, the deacetylation reaction concludes with the cleavage of the amine bond ( d 6 = 2.74 Å) in the enzyme–product (EP) complex (EP-DD, Figures A and H). This step is facilitated by HID136, which acts as a general base to accept a proton from the hydroxyl group, resulting in the formation of a negatively charged acetate ion in the binding pocket of the EP complex. Notably, the EP complex does not represent the final state of the reaction, as the product will eventually dissociate from the binding pocket. The free energy of the system can be further lowered due to the release of the translational and rotational free energy.

Through the study of Mechanisms D’D and DD’, we observe the intricate cooperative catalytic interplay between His136 and His137. By acting as proton acceptors and donors (i.e., general bases and acids) at strategic positions and stages of the reaction, they stabilize the reaction intermediates and lower the activation energy required for the deacetylation reaction to proceed efficiently.

Considering the entire free energy landscape of Mechanism DD’, the protonation of the amide nitrogen emerges as the rate-limiting step, as the TS3-DD state exhibits the highest free energy among all transition states (20.4 kcal/mol, relative to the initial ES-DD complex). However, the TS1-DD’ state, associated with the HID137-assisted water deprotonation step, also presents a significant free energy barrier of 19.7 kcal/mol. This double-peaked reaction landscape requires the system to overcome two substantial energy barriers consecutively, which generally reduces the probability of a successful reaction and results in a slower overall reaction rate compared to a single-peaked process under the same conditions (see below).

In Mechanism D’D, however, the rate-limiting step (TS3-DD) exhibits a free-energy barrier approximately 5 kcal/mol higher than the second highest barrier (TS2-D’D) and the entire free energy landscape features a standard one-peaked process. This results in a faster overall reaction rate compared to Mechanism DD’. Notably, Tyr307, a highly conserved residue across the HDAC family ( Figure S1 ), stabilizes the TS3-DD state by forming a hydrogen bond interaction with the negatively charged intermediate tetrahedron complex, and thereby facilitates the catalytic reaction. Removal of the hydroxyl group, as is shown in the Y307F variant, keeps the binding affinity for the substrate but abolishes the catalytic activity, strongly supporting the critical role of Tyr307 in the rate-limiting step.

Mechanisms D’D and DD’ share some similarities with the deacetylation mechanisms of HDAC8 proposed by Chen et al. in the presence of K + ion. In both enzymes, the reaction initiates with water deprotonation and nucleophilic attack, and may either include or omit a double-proton transfer step, which is followed by the protonation of the amide nitrogen and the cleavage of the amide bond. However, a critical distinction lies in the rate-limiting step: while HDAC8 is limited by the double-proton transfer step (analogous to TS2-D’D), HDAC10 is governed by the protonation of the substrate’s amide nitrogen (TS3-DD).

The difference arises from structural nuances between HDAC8 and HDAC10, as evidenced by their crystal structures ( Figure S10 ). A key distinction involves the conserved glycine residue (Gly145 in HDAC10; Gly151 in HDAC8). The electronegative carbonyl oxygen of this glycine is positioned farther from the substrate’s amide nitrogen in HDAC10 (3.27 Å) compared to HDAC8 (3.02 Å). The increased distance hinders protonation of the amide nitrogen, destabilizing the TS3-DD state, and thereby contributes to establishing it as the new rate-limiting step.

Additionally, we observed differences in the Zn 2+ coordination environment of HDAC8 and HDAC10. The most significant deviations occur in bond lengths d 2 , d 4 and d 5 , with absolute differences of 0.29, 0.14, and 0.19 Å, respectively ( Figure S10 ). While these coordination geometries directly influence free energy profile, their precise relationship remains complex to interpret due to the nature of coordination bonds.

The INT2-DD intermediate features a negatively charged tetrahedron structure, stabilized by a hydrogen bond with Tyr307. A proton transfer from Tyr307 to this tetrahedron intermediate generates the INT-DDY state ( Figure A), which lies only 1.2 kcal/mol higher in free energy than INT2-DD ( Figure A). No intervening transition state was identified between these intermediates, suggesting that the INT2-DD → INT-DDY transition is thermally accessible during the catalytic process. Furthermore, the INT-DDY state can bypass subsequent steps entirely by progressing directly to the enzyme–product (EP-DD) complex via TS-DDY ( Figure S11 ), defining a novel Mechanism DDY ( Figure A). However, the TS-DDY state exhibits a high activation barrier of 25.0 kcal/mol (relative to ES-DD), rendering this pathway energetically less favorable compared to Mechanism D’D.

For the mechanisms involving a preprotonated histidine (P), such as Mechanisms PD and DP, only the unprotonated histidine remains catalytically active (i.e., HID137 in ES-PD and HID136 in ES-DP). In Mechanism PD, HID137 acts as the general base to deprotonate the water molecule (ES-PD, Figure B and Figure S7A ). Unlike the concerted deprotonation/nucleophilic-attack in Mechanisms D’D and DD’, this process proceeds via two discrete steps: 1) Deprotonation generates a metastable OH – intermediate (INT1-P, Figure B and Figure S7C ), after passing through the TS1-PD transition state ( Figure S7B ); 2) The nucleophilic attack of OH – on the acetyl group occurs subsequently (TS2-P, Figure B and Figure S7D ), overcoming a high activation free energy of 26.5 kcal/mol (relative to ES-PD, Figure B). Notably, the nucleophilic attack occurs simultaneously with proton transfer from the δN atom of His136 to the carboxylic acid group of Asp172, forming INT2-P ( Figure B and Figure S7E ). This proton transfer is absent in Mechanisms D’D and DD’ but analogous to the catalytic mechanism of HDAC6. Potential energy surface scan reveals that the system’s energy is stabilized by a barrier-free proton transfer procedure ( Figure S12A ). Structural distinctions in Mechanism PD, such as electrostatic repulsion between the positively charged side chains of His137 and His136 ( Figure S12A ), likely drive this unique proton transfer step.

The final step in Mechanism PD involves protonation of the amide nitrogen on the substrate by the positively charged side chain of His137 ( Figure B). Unlike Mechanisms D’D and DD’, this step occurs concurrently with the cleavage of the amide bond in the substrate (TS3-P, Figure B and Figure S7F ). The resulting enzyme–product (EP-P) complex contains a neutral acetic acid molecule ( Figure B and Figure S7G ) as opposed to the negatively charged acetate ion observed in the EP-DD state ( Figures A and H). This difference arises because the εN position of His136 is initially protonated in Mechanism PD and cannot act as a general base to deprotonate acetic acid. The amide bond in the substrate ( d 6 ) progressively elongates from 1.33 Å (ES-PD, Figure S7A ) to 1.34 Å (INT1-P, Figure S7C ), 1.48 Å (INT2-P, Figure S7E ), and ultimately ruptures at 1.58 Å (EP-P, Figure S7G ). By comparison, d 6 is 2.74 Å in the EP-DD state. The bond length disparity ( Figure S13 ) likely reflects differences in the Zn 2+ coordination environment and local electrostatics between the two product states.

The free energy landscape of Mechanism PD identifies the nucleophilic attack by the metastable OH – as the rate-limiting step, with TS2-P presenting the highest free-energy transition state (pink solid line, Figure B). This step exhibits an activation free energy barrier of 26.5 kcal/mol (relative to the initial ES-PD state), significantly higher than that of Mechanisms D’D (20.4 kcal/mol, Figure A). The elevated barrier in Mechanism PD correlates with a markedly slower reaction rate, underscoring the critical role of active-site protonation states in modulating catalytic efficiency.

Mechanism DP diverges from Mechanism PD in its initial state, where His136 (rather than His137) acts as the general base to deprotonate the water molecule (ES-DP, Figure B and Figure S7H ). This step proceeds via transition state TS1-DP ( Figure S7I ), generating the INT1-P state with a metastable OH – that is identical to that formed in Mechanism PD ( Figure B and Figure S7C ). Beyond this point, Mechanism DP converges with Mechanism PD ( Figure B). The system overcomes the same rate-limiting TS2-P barrier (26.5 kcal/mol) during the nucleophilic attack and subsequent amide bond cleavage, ultimately yielding the EP-P product state (blue dashed line, Figure B). Notably, Mechanism DP closely resembles the catalytic mechanism of HDAC6 reported by Prejanò et al.

Analysis of the five free energy landscapes ( Figure ) indicates that Mechanism D’D is the dominant catalytic pathway, exhibiting the lowest activation free energy barrier and consequently the highest reaction rate. The protonation of the amide nitrogen on the substrate is its rate-limiting step, governing the overall kinetics of the reaction.

Steady-state kinetic measurements of HDAC10 with the substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine yielded turnover rates ( k cat ) of 0.28 s –1 for human HDAC10, 0.58 s –1 for zebrafish HDAC10, and 0.06 s –1 for trypsin treated zebrafish HDAC10 (proteolyzed at the interdomain linker for crystallization). Using the Eyring equation at 310 K, the activation free energy barriers were estimated as 19.0 kcal/mol, 18.5 kcal/mol, and 19.9 kcal/mol, respectively. The ‘humanized’ zebrafish HDAC10 variant studied here exhibits a comparable barrier. Our calculation, employing the ωB97X-D functional with zero-point energy and thermodynamic correction, predicts an activation free energy barrier of 20.4 kcal/mol ( Figure A), which aligns closely with experimental results. Additional calculations using alternative density functionals confirm that Mechanism D’D consistently exhibits the lowest activation barrier and dominates the reaction pathway ( Figure S14 and Tables S1–S3 ). The deuterium kinetic isotope effect (KIE) of the mechanism is also evaluated and the KIE value is estimated to be 3.0 (see the Methods section for details).

As for the functional role of the K + ion in HDAC10, the paralog HDAC8 maintains an analogous chemical environment in the metal coordination site, making it a physiological relevant model for elucidating the functional role of the K + ion. Experiments on HDAC8 have shown that the presence of the K + ion in the site is important for the stabilization and activation of the enzyme. Wu et al. addressed the problem by computational methods to calculate the free energy profile in the absence or presence of the K + ion in HDAC8, and found that the free energy activation barrier increases from 18.3 to 22.6 kcal/mol. Their result indicates that the K + ion contributes to activating the enzyme, in good consistency with the experimental results. They also find that the presence of the K + ion significantly increases the positive charge on Zn 2+ to make it more powerful to activate its bound water nucleophile and to polarize the carbonyl group, and increases the negative charge on δN of His143 (equivalent to His137 in HDAC10) to make it a stronger base. Both effects contribute to enhancing the catalytic activity. Because of the sequential and structural similarities between HDAC8 and HDAC10, the K + ion would play a similar functional role in HDAC10.

It is important to acknowledge the limitations of our computational methodology. We employed a quantum chemical cluster model (Model-330) to represent the active center throughout the reaction pathway, with the protein environment treated as a homogeneous dielectric continuum using PCM. Our calculations showed that the free energy profiles remain qualitatively similar when using dielectric constant ε of either 4 or 1 ( Figure S14A–C ), suggesting that our main conclusions are robust against variations in ε selection. However, the homogeneous nature of PCM imposes several limitations: (1) it cannot accurately describe atomic-level polarization effects in active sites, and (2) it fails to properly represent the dielectric gradient between protein interior (low ε) and solvent (high ε). Additionally, while we have systematically tested multiple DFT methods ( Figure S14A–C ), including B3LYP-D3­(BJ), MN15, M06-2X, PBE0-D3­(BJ) and ωB97X-D, higher-level approaches such as double-hybrid DFT can potentially provide more accurate results. Unfortunately, these more advanced methods remain computationally prohibitive for our current resources.

We next investigated the novel substrate specificity of HDAC10. As introduced earlier, HDAC10 exhibits stronger binding affinity and a higher turnover rate for N 8 -acetylspermidine compared to N 1 -acetylspermidine. To elucidate the structural basis for this divergence, we employed the independent gradient model based on Hirshfeld partition (IGMH) to analyze the ES-DD complexes using either N 8 - or N 1 -acetylspermidine as the substrate. In the N 8 -acetylspermidine complex ( Figure A), the substrate engages in strong, multifaceted interactions with the active site. Direct hydrogen bonds form between the substrate’s terminal amine group and Glu24, and between the acetyl group and Tyr307. Meanwhile, the protonated secondary amine moiety is stabilized by a sequentially unique gatekeeper residue Glu274 ( Figure S1 ) of HDAC10 through a bridging water network (orange circle, Figure A). Further stabilization is provided by van der Waals interactions with Trp205.

IGMH analysis (isovalue = 0.008 au) for the weak interaction between HDAC10 and N 8 -acetylspermidine (A) and between HDAC10 and N 1 -acetylspermidine (B), respectively. Orange circles show Glu274, two bridging water molecules, substrate, and His176. Red arrows indicate the interactions between the substrate and two water molecules.

In contrast, the N 1 -acetylspermidine based ES-DD complex ( Figure B) exhibits significantly weaker binding affinity, attributed to the absence of a water-mediated hydrogen-bond network (red arrows, Figure B). This disruption destabilizes interactions with the secondary amine moiety and significantly reduces substrate binding strength.

Building on these structural insights into substrate binding, we further elucidated the physical origins of enzyme–substrate interactions through energy decomposition analysis. The total binding energy was partitioned into four components: electrostatic, exchange-repulsion, orbital, and dispersion energy ( Figure A). Comparative analysis revealed that N 8 -acetylspermidine exhibits stronger binding (−222.7 kcal/mol) than N 1 -acetylspermidine (−206.1 kcal/mol). This enhanced affinity primarily stems from more favorable electrostatic interaction (−279.4 kcal/mol vs −245.2 kcal/mol) and orbital energy contributions (−163.0 kcal/mol vs −138.1 kcal/mol). However, these gains are partially offset by increased exchange-repulsion energy in the N 8 -acetylspermidine complex ( Figure A), likely due to closer contact between N 1 -acetylspermidine and active-site residues such as Trp205 (see below).

(A) Energy decomposition analysis for the binding energy between HDAC10 and substrate N 8 -acetylspermidine and N 1 -acetylspermidine, respectively (els, electrostatic; xrep, exchange-repulsion; orb, orbital; disp, dispersion). (B) Residue contribution to the binding energy in the ES-DD and ES’-DD complexes. The energetic contribution of Glu274 incorporates the stabilization effects from the two associated bridging water molecules. The catalytic water molecule coordinated with the Zn 2+ ion is considered a part of the substrate.

Residue-level energy decomposition clarifies the structural origins of HDAC10’s substrate specificity, with Glu274 and its water network driving the substrate selectivity ( Figure B). These components favor N 8 -acetylspermidine by 23.8 kcal/mol over N 1 -acetylspermidine, a stark contrast that aligns with the critical water-mediated interactions observed in the N 8 -acetylspermidine based ES-DD complex ( Figure A). This dominance underscores Glu274’s role as the key selectivity determinant, far surpassing contributions from direct-contact residues (Glu24, Tyr307, and Trp205). Glu24 and Tyr307 show a slight preference (∼1 kcal/mol difference), and Trp205 even weakly favors N 1 -acetylspermidine by 6 kcal/mol due to a newly established cation-π interaction.

To complement our structural and thermodynamic analyses, we performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of HDAC10 bound to N 8 -acetylspermidine or N 1 -acetylspermidine ( Figure S15A,B ). Root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) profiles derived from simulations showed qualitative agreement with crystallographic B-factors ( Figure S15C ), validating our simulation protocols (as detailed in the Methods section). Strikingly, N 8 -acetylspermidine remained stably bound across three independent 1000-ns trajectories ( Figure S15D ), whereas N 1 -acetylspermidine dissociated in two of three replicates ( Figure S15E ). This dynamic instability aligns with the kinetic measurements showing N 1 -acetylspermidine’s higher K M value (weaker binding affinity), further corroborating the critical role of HDAC10’s active-site architecture. Notably, the water-mediated network between N 8 -acetylspermidine and Glu274 is well kept during MD simulation ( Figure S15F ), providing important contribution to discriminate the substrate.

Besides its weakened binding affinity, kinetic experiments reveal that N 1 -acetylspermidine exhibits a significantly reduced turnover rate ( k cat ) compared to N 8 -acetylspermidine. To uncover the origin of this catalytic inefficiency, we mapped the free energy landscape for N 1 -acetylspermidine deacetylation ( Figure and Figure S16 ). Following Mechanism D’D, the activation free energy barrier rises to 23.1 kcal/mol (vs 20.4 kcal/mol for N 8 -acetylspermidine), a trend consistent across multiple DFT functionals ( Figure S14C ). The rate-limiting step remains protonation of the amide nitrogen of the substrate (TS3′-DD, Figure ), but the elevated barrier reflects a critical structural distinction: the protonated secondary amine moiety is closer to the catalytic active site in N 1 -acetylspermidine, increasing electrostatic repulsion with the transferred proton during TS3′-DD formation.

This dual mechanismweaker binding (higher K M ) and higher catalytic barrier (lower k cat )explains HDAC10’s pronounced preference for N 8 -acetylspermidine. The enzyme’s active-site architecture thus enforces substrate selectivity at both the thermodynamic (binding) and kinetic (catalysis) levels.
sections.conclusion: HDAC10 distinguishes itself within the HDAC family for its unique substrate specificity and catalytic mechanism. By employing a 330-atom quantum mechanical cluster model, this study deciphers the molecular basis of HDAC10’s activity, revealing the double-proton mechanism D’D as dominant, with protonation of the amide nitrogen of substrate being the rate-limiting step (20.4 kcal/mol barrier). Substrate selectivity arises from a dual-filter mechanism: N 8 -acetylspermidine benefits from stronger binding (mainly via Glu274’s water-mediated network and Glu24/Tyr307 interactions) and a lower catalytic barrier compared to N 1 -acetylspermidine, which suffers from electrostatic repulsion and weakened protein–substrate interactions. Crucially, this work identifies Glu274’s bridging water network, Glu24 and Tyr307 as key structural determinants for rational drug design. Collectively, these insights resolve HDAC10’s substrate discrimination at atomic resolution, bridging structural, thermodynamic, and kinetic data to advance the development of isoform-specific inhibitors. By highlighting HDAC10’s unique catalytic landscape, this study opens avenues for targeting its dysregulation in diseases like cancer.
